indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B6.5.1.1 Recognise the importance of personal hygiene

skills.description: Explain what minimising waste means (reducing the amount of waste produced).
Identify types of waste produced at home, school and community.
Describe ways to minimise waste (e.g. reuse, recycle, avoid single-use plastics, compost food waste).
Suggest waste minimisation measures for different places (classroom, home, market, hospital).
Explain why minimising waste is important for the environment and health.
Plan and design a litterbin for the class or school community.

spec.difficultyPlan: 20 questions total — Difficulty 1: 5; Difficulty 2: 7; Difficulty 3: 5; Difficulty 4: 3.
misconceptions: Waste minimisation means burning all waste.
Reusing items is not minimising waste.
Composting food waste is not useful.
Litterbins are not part of waste minimisation.

questions.stem: What does minimising waste mean?
options: Reducing the amount of waste produced
hints: Think about using less and reusing items.
questions.explanation: Minimising waste means reducing the amount of waste we produce.
questions.misconception: Waste minimisation means burning all waste.

questions.stem: What is waste minimisation?
answer: reducing the amount of waste produced
questions.explanation: Waste minimisation is reducing the amount of waste we produce by using less, reusing items and recycling.
questions.misconception: Waste minimisation means making more waste.

questions.stem: Which of these is a type of waste?
hints: Which item is thrown away after use?
questions.explanation: A plastic bottle is a type of waste. It is thrown away after use.
questions.misconception: Only factories produce waste.

questions.stem: Name two types of waste produced at home.
hints: Think about what you throw away.
Food waste and plastic are common.
questions.explanation: Common types of waste at home include paper, plastic, food waste, bottles and cans.
questions.misconception: Only factories produce waste.

questions.stem: Which of these is a way to minimise waste?
hints: It stops waste from piling up.
questions.explanation: Reusing plastic bags is a way to minimise waste because it reduces the amount of waste produced.
questions.misconception: Burning all waste is the best way to minimise waste.

questions.stem: What does 'recycle' mean?
options: Making new things from used materials
hints: Recycling turns old things into new things.
Think about plastic bottles being made into new items.
questions.explanation: Recycling means making new things from used materials, which helps minimise waste.
questions.misconception: Recycling is the same as throwing waste away.

questions.stem: How can a school minimise waste in the classroom?
options: Use a bin for paper and plastic
hints: Waste should go into a bin.
questions.explanation: Using a bin for paper and plastic helps minimise waste in the classroom by keeping it tidy and making recycling easier.
questions.misconception: Throwing waste on the floor is acceptable.

questions.stem: Give one way to minimise waste at home.
hints: Composting food waste is one way.
questions.explanation: Ways to minimise waste at home include reusing containers, composting food waste, avoiding single-use plastics and recycling paper.
questions.misconception: Waste cannot be minimised at home.

questions.stem: Why is minimising waste important?
questions.explanation: Minimising waste is important because it keeps the environment clean and reduces pollution.
questions.misconception: Minimising waste is not important.

questions.stem: Design a simple litterbin for your classroom using local materials. Label the materials you would use and write one sentence explaining how it will help minimise waste.

criteria.description: Drew a simple design of a litterbin
Labeled at least one suitable local material
Explained how the litterbin helps minimise waste

hints: Think about using cardboard, plastic or wood.
A litterbin keeps waste in one place.
questions.explanation: This is a drawing task. Your teacher will mark it using the rubric.
questions.misconception: Litterbins are not part of waste minimisation.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes minimising waste?
options: Reducing waste by using less and reusing items
questions.explanation: Minimising waste means reducing waste by using less and reusing items.
questions.misconception: Minimising waste means increasing waste.

questions.stem: Which of these is food waste?
hints: It is the skin of a fruit.
questions.explanation: A banana peel is food waste.
questions.misconception: Food waste is not a type of waste.

questions.stem: Give one way to reuse waste.
answer: use plastic bottles as plant pots
hints: Plastic bottles can be used as plant pots.
questions.explanation: One way to reuse waste is to use plastic bottles as plant pots.
questions.misconception: Reusing items is not minimising waste.

questions.stem: A market produces a lot of waste. Which action best minimises waste?
options: Encourage traders to use reusable bags
hints: Burning and throwing waste in drains cause problems.
questions.explanation: Encouraging traders to use reusable bags helps minimise waste at the market.
questions.misconception: Burning all waste is the best way to minimise waste.

questions.stem: Explain why minimising waste is important for the community.
answer: it keeps the community clean and reduces disease
it reduces pollution and saves resources
questions.explanation: Minimising waste is important for the community because it keeps the environment clean, reduces disease and saves resources.
questions.misconception: Minimising waste has no benefit.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of reducing waste?
hints: Buying only what you need prevents waste.
questions.explanation: Buying only what you need is an example of reducing waste because it prevents unnecessary items from becoming waste.
questions.misconception: Buying extra food reduces waste.

questions.stem: How can a hospital minimise waste?
questions.explanation: A hospital can minimise waste by using reusable equipment where it is safe to do so.
questions.misconception: Hospitals cannot minimise waste.

questions.stem: Plan three steps to make a litterbin for your classroom using local materials. Write each step clearly.

criteria.description: Wrote three clear steps for making a litterbin
Steps are realistic and use local materials
Plan is neat and easy to follow

hints: Then placing it in the classroom.
questions.explanation: This is a written task. Your teacher will mark it using the rubric.
questions.misconception: Planning a litterbin is not useful.

questions.stem: Why is it important to label a litterbin (e.g. 'Plastics Only')?
answer: to help people put waste in the correct bin
hints: Labels help people know where to put waste.
questions.explanation: Labelling a litterbin is important because it helps people put the correct type of waste in it, making waste separation and recycling easier.
questions.misconception: Labels on litterbins are not important.

questions.stem: A pupil says, 'Minimising waste is only the job of the government.' What is the best correction?
options: Only the government can minimise waste
hints: Think about what you can do at home and school.
Everyone produces waste, so everyone can help.
questions.explanation: Everyone can help minimise waste by reusing items, recycling and avoiding single-use plastics.
questions.misconception: Only the government can minimise waste.
